facts.claim: Deezer credits "Pain and Misery" to Brendon Love, Joshua Teskey, Liam Gough and Samuel Teskey as writers and composers.
The Teskey Brothers formed in 2008. The members are brothers Josh Teskey (vocals) and Sam Teskey (guitar), with Brendon Love (bass) and Liam Gough (drums).
"Pain and Misery" was the first single from the album Half Mile Harvest. The band released it in 2016, before the album came out on 12 January 2017.
Half Mile Harvest was recorded at the band's home studio, Half Mile Harvest Studios, in Warrandyte. Josh Teskey says his brother Sam was the main engineer.
Sam Teskey built the analogue studio himself. His Studer A800 tape machine is at the core of the studio and the album, and the band chose to record to it deliberately.
The band released the album with no management and no label. Josh said they recorded music they loved in the way they loved to record it.

A 2016 CD EP titled "Pain And Misery" was released on Half Mile Harvest Recordings and recorded at Half Mile Harvest Studios. It also contains "Love Her With A Feeling", "Rats In My Kitchen" and "Sweet Sixteen".
Beat magazine reports that after the band released "Pain and Misery" as a single, the local record store sold out. The band then restocked its shelves with copies of Half Mile Harvest.

Atwood Magazine says the song is a heartbreak track with a 1960s American soul-inspired sound. It says the band was re-releasing the album in a deluxe edition on 26 October 2018 through Glassnote/Decca.

Half Mile Harvest is the band's debut album. It reached number 18 on the ARIA chart and topped the ARIA Independent Album chart. Their later albums are Run Home Slow (2019) and The Winding Way (2023).

research.lineage: The song sits in the 1960s American soul and blues tradition, with critics comparing the band to Stax Records acts and Otis Redding, and it comes from the Warrandyte/Melbourne scene.

draft:
The chorus of **Pain and Misery** begs someone to stay who has already gone. That's the whole knot of the song: a plea for presence wrapped around a plain report of absence. The narrator isn't building a case or trying to win anyone back with reasons. They're still asking after the answer has been given.

Josh Teskey sings it in a slightly raspy voice, holding long notes and then breaking into short, bluesy phrases, the way someone talks when they've rehearsed what to say and can't get through it. A second voice sits above him in a higher register, and that harmony makes the begging sound a little less alone than the words claim to be. Underneath, the band keeps a relaxed shuffle at a medium-slow pace. A walking bass line moves under a snare that lands on the backbeat, while a clean electric guitar rolls out arpeggiated chords and small fills between the lines. Nobody hurries, and the groove holds steady so the singer can come apart on top of it.

The lyric is built from old soul stock: honey, baby, love as a crazy game. Some of it is familiar to the point of being worn. But the second verse turns. "Sometimes I curse that day of when you came along," he sings, then: "I was happy." It's not clear whether he means happy before her or happy with her, and the song doesn't need to choose. Resentment and longing sit in the same breath, and neither cancels the other. Then comes the line that shows how big the loss really is: "Now that I've lost the best friend that I ever had." It isn't only a lover who's gone. By the last lines the reasoning drops away entirely, leaving bare want and need, repeated.

Critics have compared the band to Stax acts and Otis Redding, and the debt to 1960s American soul is open. All four members share the writing credit: brothers Josh and Sam Teskey with bassist Brendon Love and drummer Liam Gough. They cut it at Half Mile Harvest Studios, the analogue room Sam built himself in Warrandyte, outside Melbourne. He engineered the sessions and chose to record to a Studer A800 tape machine. The band had no label and no management. When they put the song out as the first single from their debut, Half Mile Harvest, the local record store sold out, and the band restocked the shelves with the album. You can hear that home-built warmth in the room sound, live and slightly raw.

The song sticks because it lets you sit inside the moment after someone leaves, when you're still pleading with an empty doorway and a steady band is the only thing holding you up.
